item.title: Local AI Session Manager Runs in a Single 138 MB Rust Binary
item.description:
Local AI Session Manager Runs in a Single 138 MB Rust Binary

A new self‑reflective AI session manager can run entirely locally from one Rust binary of about 138 MB, embedding SQLite and a vector index, and requiring no containers, database servers, Python, or API keys.

🔍 Overview

  • Single executable (~138 MB) written in Rust
  • Embedded SQLite stores chunks, embeddings, and enrichment state
  • In‑memory HNSW vector index for fast local search
  • FastEmbed provides 384‑dimensional local embeddings
  • No external dependencies such as Docker, database servers, or API keys

🧩 How it Works

  • Sessions start with a concise recap paragraph that states intent, completed work, settled items, open items, and the next step.
  • Every clause in a session can carry a receipt linking to a commit, task, verdict, or correction; clauses without evidence are omitted.
  • Dreams: the system checks past conclusions against git history and marks stale anchors with the commit that changed them.
  • Compaction: after a compact, the system stores pointers to the original turns and can retrieve them via csr_transcript.
  • A companion pane shows what the AI was told, what it missed, and any user corrections.
  • The plumbing layer uses SQLite and a local vector index to search past sessions; the AI can invoke this directly through MCP tools.

⚙️ Key Details

  • CI on 2026‑11‑18: cargo test --locked --no-fail-fast → 6,939 passed, 0 failed, 34 ignored
  • cargo fmt, clippy -D warnings, and actionlint report no issues
  • Installer tests pass 58 of 58
  • Repo can be scanned manually with csr-engine codemap scan --repo <path>
  • Local vector search and embedding generation require zero external services

🚀 Availability

  • The binary runs locally in a single process; no Docker, no remote services, and no API keys are needed.
  • Users can map a repository to enable code‑aware answers across all worktrees.
  • The system integrates with Claude via the Self‑Reflect plugin to maintain session continuity.

#AI #Rust #LocalLLM #SelfReflect #DeveloperTools

Source: ramakay/claude-self-reflect

item.title: Simple Python bindings for llama.cpp released
item.description:
Simple Python bindings for llama.cpp released

Simple Python bindings for the llama.cpp library are now available, providing low-level access to the C API via ctypes and a high-level Python API for text completion.

🧩 How it works

The package allows developers to integrate llama.cpp into Python environments with several key interfaces:

  • Low-level access: Direct access to the C API through a ctypes interface.
  • High-level API: A Python API designed for text completion.
  • OpenAI-like API: Compatibility with standard OpenAI-style interfaces.
  • Framework Support: Includes compatibility with LangChain and LlamaIndex.
  • Web Server: Features an OpenAI compatible web server.

⚙️ Key details

The server component supports a range of additional capabilities, including:

  • Function Calling support
  • Vision API support for multimodal models
  • Configuration and multi-model support
  • Local Copilot replacement for code completion

Installation requires Python 3.8+ and a C compiler. The build process compiles llama.cpp from source and installs it alongside the Python package. Hardware acceleration backends are supported via specific environment variables:

  • OpenBLAS: Set GGML_BLAS and GGML_BLAS_VENDOR.
  • CUDA: Set GGML_CUDA=on. Supported CUDA versions include 11.8, 12.1, 12.2, 12.3, 12.4, 12.5, 13.0, or 13.2. GPU compute capability requirements vary by version: 6.0–8.9 for CUDA 11.8, 6.0+ for CUDA 12, and 7.5+ for CUDA 13. Pre-built wheels for CUDA support Python 3.10, 3.11, or 3.12.
  • Metal (MPS): Set GGML_METAL=on. Requires macOS 11.0 or later.

All llama.cpp cmake build options can be configured via the CMAKE_ARGS environment variable or the --config-settings / -C CLI flag during installation.

🚀 Availability

Documentation is available at https://llama-cpp-python.readthedocs.io/en/latest. Installation is supported on Linux (gcc or clang), Windows (Visual Studio or MinGW), and MacOS (Xcode).

#llama.cpp #Python #Llama #LocalLLM #CTypes

Source: abetlen/llama-cpp-python

item.title: MLX-Serve enables local AI on Macs and iPhones with OpenAI compatibility
item.description:
MLX-Serve enables local AI on Macs and iPhones with OpenAI compatibility

MLX-Serve is a native application and local server for macOS that allows users to run open models locally for chat, coding agents, image generation, video, music, speech, and 3D tasks. It speaks the OpenAI, Anthropic, and Ollama APIs, runs offline, requires no Python or account, and is MIT licensed.

🚀 Availability

  • macOS: Requires macOS 26.2 or later on Apple Silicon. It includes a native app and a local server listening on http://localhost:11234.
  • iPhone: An extension called MLX-Serve puts the engine on iPhone, supporting A17 Pro-class devices or newer running iOS 26.
  • Linux: Release downloads are available for NVIDIA GPUs, supporting x64 for RTX 20 to 50 cards, and arm64 for DGX Spark, GH200, and Jetson Thor.
  • Windows: A script is provided to build it on Windows systems with NVIDIA cards.
  • Licensing: The project is MIT licensed.

💡 Why it matters

The tool provides a unified local endpoint that supports multiple API standards simultaneously. This allows users to connect existing OpenAI, Anthropic, or Ollama clients to local models without cloud dependencies.

⚙️ Key details

API and Model Support

  • Supports OpenAI chat, completions, and Responses; Anthropic Messages; and Ollama APIs.
  • Features include streaming, tool calls, JSON schemas, vision, and reasoning.
  • Compatible with any MLX model with a supported architecture and any GGUF format.
  • Specific models supported include GLM-5.3-Flash and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (runnable on a 128 GB Mac by reading experts from the SSD).
  • Generative models available in the app or over HTTP include FLUX.2, Qwen-Image, Krea, MOSS-Image, LTX-Video, MiniMax-H3, ACE-Step, YuE2, Qwen3-TTS with voice cloning, and Hunyuan3D.
  • Speech-to-text is supported in 30 languages with word timings and speaker identification.

Performance and Hardware

  • Mac Clustering: Two Macs connected via a Thunderbolt 5 cable can run one model together; Macs on a network can also use each other’s models.
  • Speed Improvements: On an M4 Max, models decode 10% to 51% faster in v26.11.1 compared to v26.8.
  • Integration: mlx-serve launch claude starts Claude Code against the local Mac, configured with the model’s actual context window.
  • Updates: The application updates itself automatically and suggests models that fit the specific Mac.

🔍 Overview

The server provides a built-in web console accessible by opening the local address in a browser. It is designed to run offline, removing the need for cloud accounts or Python environments.

#MLX-Serve #LocalLLM #AppleSilicon #OpenAI #Mac

Source: hekmon/comfyui-openai-api Source: ddalcu/mlx-serve

item.title: Qwen 3.8 27B Runs Locally on a Laptop, Interpreting Model Weights
item.description:
Qwen 3.8 27B Runs Locally on a Laptop, Interpreting Model Weights

A new update shows that the Qwen 3.8 27B large language model can be run on a typical laptop and is capable of interpreting its own model weights.

🔍 Overview

  • On 3 November 2026, the author reported that Qwen 3.8 27B was successfully executed on a laptop.
  • The model was able to interpret its own weights during this local inference.

🧩 How it works

  • The demonstration involved loading the 27‑billion‑parameter Qwen 3.8 model on consumer‑grade hardware.
  • Weight interpretation functionality was verified as part of the run.

⚙️ Key details

  • Model: Qwen 3.8 27B
  • Hardware: Laptop (specific specs not disclosed)
  • Capability: Local execution with weight interpretation

🚀 Availability

  • The observation was made on 3 November 2026; no formal release notes or distribution details are provided in the evidence.

💡 Why it matters

  • Demonstrates that models of this size can be operated without large‑scale server infrastructure.
  • Shows progress in making high‑capacity LLMs more accessible for on‑device experimentation.

#Qwen #LocalLLM #ModelWeights

Source: Release: datasette-llm 0.1a10

item.title: 🚀 Devstral-Small-2505: The Open-Source Lightweight Coding Agent That Outperforms GPT-4.1 Mini
item.description:
🚀 Devstral-Small-2505: The Open-Source Lightweight Coding Agent That Outperforms GPT-4.1 Mini

Summary: Discover Mistral AI and All Hands AI’s groundbreaking collaborative creation - Devstral-Small-2505. This compact 24B parameter model runs locally on consumer hardware yet crushes SWE-Bench benchmarks with 46.8% verified score, making it the #1 open-source model for software engineering tasks. Learn how to deploy and use this Apache 2.0 licensed coding assistant with multiple deployment options.

🤖 Meet Devstral: A New Champion in Agentic Coding

The software development landscape has just shifted dramatically with the release of Devstral-Small-2505, a revolutionary lightweight model that punches far above its weight class. As a collaboration between Mistral AI and All Hands AI, this specialized model represents a significant milestone in accessible, powerful coding assistance.

What makes Devstral particularly exciting is its focus on 𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗰 𝗰𝗼𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 - the ability to actively explore codebases, edit multiple files simultaneously, and power sophisticated software engineering workflows. Unlike general-purpose LLMs, Devstral was specifically fine-tuned from Mistral-Small-3.1 with software engineering tasks in mind.

The results speak for themselves: Devstral achieves a remarkable 46.8% score on SWE-Bench Verified, outperforming the previous open-source state-of-the-art by 6%. More impressively, it beats GPT-4.1-mini by a massive margin (46.8% vs 23.6%) and even edges out Claude 3.5 Haiku (40.6%).

💻 Small Size, Big Capabilities

Perhaps the most compelling aspect of Devstral is its accessibility. With just 24 billion parameters, you can run this model locally on:

  • A single RTX 4090
  • A Mac with 32GB RAM
  • Other consumer-grade hardware

This lightweight profile doesn’t come at the expense of capabilities:

  • 🔍 Massive Context Window: 128k tokens let Devstral understand large codebases
  • 🔤 Advanced Tokenizer: Tekken tokenizer with 131k vocabulary for efficient code representation
  • 📜 Apache 2.0 License: Full commercial and non-commercial use permissions
  • 🛠️ Tool Usage: Built specifically to excel at using software tools for exploration and modification

The removal of the vision encoder from the base Mistral-Small-3.1 model focuses Devstral entirely on text-based software engineering tasks, resulting in more efficient performance for its intended purpose.

🔧 Getting Started with Devstral

There are several ways to use Devstral in your development workflow. Let’s explore the most accessible approaches.

𝗕𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗢𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻: 𝗢𝗽𝗲𝗻𝗛𝗮𝗻𝗱𝘀 𝗦𝗰𝗮𝗳𝗳𝗼𝗹𝗱

For the optimal experience with Devstral, the OpenHands scaffold is recommended. You can use it through Mistral’s API or by running it locally.

Using Mistral’s API:

  1. Create a Mistral account and obtain an API key
  2. Set up OpenHands through a Docker container:
1
2
3

export MISTRAL_API_KEY=<MY_KEY>
docker pull docker.all-hands.dev/all-hands-ai/runtime:0.39-nikolaik
# Additional setup commands...

Running Locally:

  1. Launch a vLLM server:
1

vllm serve mistralai/Devstral-Small-2505 --tokenizer_mode mistral --config_format mistral --load_format mistral --tool-call-parser mistral --enable-auto-tool-choice --tensor-parallel-size 2
  1. Set up OpenHands Docker container
  2. Connect via localhost:3000 and configure with your server URL

📸 See the code examples in the original documentation for exact Docker commands and configuration.

𝗔𝗹𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗗𝗲𝗽𝗹𝗼𝘆𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗢𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀

If OpenHands isn’t your preferred workflow, several other deployment options are available:

  • vLLM: Recommended for production-ready inference pipelines
  • mistral-inference: Best for quick “vibe checks” and experimentation
  • Transformers Library: For custom Python integration
  • LM Studio: For a GUI-based local deployment
  • llama.cpp: For optimized CPU inference
  • Ollama: For simplified deployment with ollama run devstral

Each integration method provides different trade-offs between ease of setup, performance, and customization options.

🏆 Practical Example: Building a Todo App

Let’s see Devstral in action with a practical example - building a Todo list application from scratch.

When prompted to build a Todo app with specific requirements (FastAPI backend, React frontend, SQLite database), Devstral can:

  1. Generate the complete application architecture
  2. Create backend API endpoints with proper data models
  3. Implement the React frontend components
  4. Set up database connections and migrations
  5. Provide deployment instructions

The remarkable aspect is how Devstral can handle multi-file projects coherently, understanding the relationships between different components and maintaining consistency across the codebase.

Once the initial app is generated, you can iterate on it through natural language requests:

  • “Add checkbox UI elements instead of click-to-mark”
  • “Implement filtering by task status”
  • “Add task editing functionality”

📸 See the Todo app example in action through the OpenHands scaffold.

🧠 Real-World Use Case: Test Coverage Analysis

Another impressive demonstration of Devstral’s capabilities is its ability to analyze test coverage in existing codebases.

In the example provided, Devstral was connected to the mistral-common repository and instructed to check test coverage and create visualizations. The agent:

  1. Browsed the codebase to understand test configuration
  2. Set up testing dependencies
  3. Launched coverage tests
  4. Wrote code to visualize the results
  5. Generated multiple plot types showing coverage metrics

This type of analysis typically requires significant domain knowledge and coding skill, yet Devstral handled it smoothly through natural language instructions.

🚀 Why Devstral Matters

What makes Devstral truly groundbreaking is how it democratizes access to elite AI coding assistance. While models like GPT-4 and Claude 3.5 Opus offer impressive capabilities, they remain accessible only through APIs with usage costs and potential privacy concerns.

Devstral brings competitive performance to local environments with its Apache 2.0 license, making advanced coding assistance available to individual developers, small teams, and organizations with limited resources.

The gap between Devstral’s 46.8% SWE-Bench score and GPT-4.1-mini’s 23.6% demonstrates that open-source models can not just compete with but significantly outperform some commercial offerings.

As software development continues to grow in complexity, tools like Devstral will play an increasingly vital role in boosting developer productivity, reducing barriers to entry, and democratizing access to AI assistance.
